notes.short: “An outstretched arm” stands for God's power
notes.about: God promises to redeem Israel “with an outstretched arm.” Since a man's strength lies so largely in his arms, the arm spoken of God stands for His mighty power, stretched out in His judgments to strike Egypt and set Israel free.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's mighty power, stretched out in judgment against Egypt to set Israel free

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: arms are given to God for His strength and power, which in men lies so largely in the arms. F. C. Cook (Barnes' Notes) calls it a common figure, the more forceful to men who knew the Egyptian sign showing might by two outstretched arms. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) says God stretches out His arm when He goes forth in judgment to smite the rebellious.

cites.quote: Arms are attributed to God, to indicate His strength and power, which in men lies so largely in the arms.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: With a stretched out arm - The figure is common and quite intelligible; it may have struck Moses and the people the more forcibly since they were familiar with the hieroglyphic which represents might by two outstretched arms.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: for God raises, stretches out His arm, when He proceeds in judgment to smite the rebellious. These expressions repeat with greater emphasis the "strong hand" of Exo 6:1, and are frequently connected with it in the rhetorical language of Deuteronomy
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “Consecrate” means: declare them set apart to God
notes.about: God tells Moses to consecrate every firstborn male. The act is put for the word that declares it: Moses is to tell the people that the firstborn belong to the LORD, as he does in verse 12, “you are to present to the LORD the firstborn male of every womb.”

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.part: of the Subject: the act put for declaring it
figure.means: a word Moses is to speak: he is to tell the people, in God's name, that every firstborn male is set apart to Him

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Subject, where an act is put for the declaration of it: Moses is to declare in God's name that He sets the firstborn apart, which Moses did in verses 11 and 12. F. C. Cook (Barnes' Notes) says the command to Moses was to declare God's will that the firstborn be consecrated; Poole reads it as a command to the people to sanctify them.
notes.limit: The writers word it a little differently: Moses declares that God sets the firstborn apart, or he commands the people to give them to God.

cites.quote: “Sanctify unto me all the first-born”: i.e., declare in My name to the People that I sanctify (i.e., separate) them, etc. Which Moses did in verses 11 and 12.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: The command is addressed to Moses. It was to declare the will of God that all firstborn were to be consecrated to Him, set apart from all other creatures.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: And sanctify, i.e. command all the people to sanctify, as Moses did, Exodus 13:12
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/exodus/13.htm

notes.short: The feast is “a sign for you on your hand”
notes.about: The feast is called a sign on the hand and a reminder on the forehead. Like a band or ring worn where it is always seen, it was to keep the LORD's deliverance from Egypt always in mind, so that His law would be on their lips.

figure.name: Metaphor
figure.words: a sign for you on your hand and a reminder on your forehead
figure.means: the feast keeps what the LORD did always before Israel, as plainly as a band or ring on the hand or the forehead is seen

original.note: In Hebrew the reminder is between your eyes, which the BSB gives as “on your forehead”.

notes.evidence: F. C. Cook (Barnes' Notes) takes the words metaphorically: the facts of the Passover kept in mind as though written on parchment fastened on the wrists or between the eyes. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls them a figurative, proverbial expression for keeping the precept always in mind. Calvin says Moses uses a comparison: their redemption set before their eyes, as a ring on the finger is seen.
notes.limit: Writers differ on whether real bands were also to be worn on the wrist and forehead. They agree the words call Israel to keep the deliverance always in mind.

cites.quote: other commentators are generally agreed that it is to be understood metaphorically. … They were to keep all the facts of the Passover constantly in mind, and, referring to a custom prevalent ages before Moses in Egypt, to have them present as though they were inscribed on papyrus or parchment fastened on the wrists, or on the face between the eyes.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The words are then used figuratively, as a proverbial expression employed to give emphasis to the injunction to bear this precept continually in mind, to be always mindful to observe it.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: uses a comparison when he says, “it shall be for a sign unto thee upon thine hand, and for a memorial between thine eyes;” as though it had been said that their redemption should be set before their eyes in the passover, just as the ring which is on the finger, or the ornament which is bound upon the forehead are constantly seen.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Year after year”: in Hebrew, days put for a year
notes.about: The BSB gives “year after year” for Hebrew words that speak of days. Days, a part of the year, are put for the whole year: Israel was to keep the feast at its appointed time every year.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.part: of the Part: a part of time for the whole
figure.means: in Hebrew, days: days, a part of the year, are put for a whole year, so the feast is kept every year

original.note: In Hebrew the words are mi-yamim yamimah, from days to days, both from yom, “day”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Part, a part of time put for the whole, where days are put for a full year, and reads it as from year to year. Poole notes that the Hebrew says from days to days, and that days in Hebrew are often put for a complete year.

cites.quote: “Thou wilt therefore keep this ordinance at its appointed season: from days to days”: i.e., from year to year.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Heb. From days to days. But days in the Hebrew tongue are oft put for a complete year.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/exodus/13.htm

notes.short: One animal, the donkey, named for all unclean ones
notes.about: Only the donkey is named, but the rule covered the firstborn of every unclean animal, which could not be offered in sacrifice. Numbers 18:15 speaks of “every firstborn male of unclean animals.” The donkey, likely named as the most common of them, stands for them all.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.part: of the Species: one kind put for the whole class
figure.means: the firstborn of every unclean animal, which could not be offered in sacrifice and so had to be redeemed

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Species: the firstborn of all unclean animals had to be redeemed (Numbers 18:15), but only one kind is named. Clarke infers the donkey is put for unclean animals in general. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) has it stand for all of them, as the most common; Poole says it alone is named for all the rest, as most common and useful.

cites.quote: “And every firstling of an ass thou shalt redeem with a lamb.” The firstborn of all unclean beasts, which might not be sacrificed, had to be redeemed (see Num 18:15), but only one species is named here, and in 34:20.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Hence we may infer that ass is put here for any unclean beast, or for unclean beasts in general.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: asses, as the most common of the unclean domestic animals, instead of the whole of these animals, Num 18:15
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: The ass was an unclean creature, and therefore this rule was to be observed in all other unclean creatures, as appears, … The ass alone is here named for all the rest, because this creature was most common, and most useful, and yet was not to be spared
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/exodus/13.htm

notes.short: Pharaoh's “army” is, in Hebrew, his power
notes.about: In Hebrew Pharaoh's army is called his strength or power. The army is named for what it showed, his might, and by means of that army the LORD would gain honor.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.means: Pharaoh's army, named by a word for his power, which the army showed

original.note: In Hebrew “army” is chayil, a word for strength or power.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Adjunct in Figures of Speech: the Hebrew says his power, which is put for his army, the army being the expression of his power.

cites.quote: “And I will be honoured upon Pharaoh and upon all his power.” ... his power, which is put by Metonymy for his army, which was the expression of his power.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: “My song”: the LORD is the One the song praises
notes.about: The LORD is called “my song” because He is the One the song is about: His saving help gives His people their reason to praise. The same words come back in Psalm 118:14 and Isaiah 12:2.

figure.name: Metonymy
figure.means: the One whom I praise in my song, the subject of my praise

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Metonymy of the Adjunct in Figures of Speech: my song means He whom I praise in my song. Poole calls the LORD the matter or subject of the song of praise, and Calvin says His grace gives the people just ground for praise.

cites.quote: “The Lord is my strength and song”: i.e., He whom I praise in my song.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: My strength and song; the matter or subject of the present song of praise.
cites.read: Bible Hub's transcription, at https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/exodus/15.htm

cites.quote: In this expression they acknowledge that they have a sufficient defense in God; and afterwards they add, that His grace furnishes them with just ground for praise.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: “Praise Him” is said again as “exalt Him”
notes.about: The verse ends with two matching lines, each naming God and then vowing praise. “I will praise Him” is answered by “I will exalt Him,” and the match helps settle what the first word means.

lines.words: He is my God, and I will praise Him,
my father’s God, and I will exalt Him.

notes.evidence: George Rawlinson (Ellicott's Commentary) says the law of parallelism requires the word rendered praise to mean glorify, so that it answers the exalt of the next clause.
notes.limit: Some older versions read the word for praise as preparing Him a dwelling place; the matching line favours praise.

cites.quote: The law of parallelism also requires such a meaning as “glorify” to correspond with the “exalt” of the next clause.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

notes.short: God's “right hand” stands for His mighty power
notes.about: The song speaks of the LORD's right hand, a part of the human body spoken of God. It stands for His almighty power, which alone broke Pharaoh's army at the sea, with no help from man.

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.words: Your right hand, O LORD, has shattered the enemy
figure.means: the LORD's almighty power, which alone broke the enemy at the sea

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia: a right hand is given to God to show the highest power. Clarke reads it as God's omnipotence, and Henry as an act of His power and not Israel's. Calvin says the right hand is named twice to show the miracle could not be put down to chance or to the efforts of man.

cites.quote: A Right Hand is attributed to God; to denote the highest power, and most Divine authority.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: Thy right hand - Thy omnipotence, manifested in a most extraordinary way.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: All this was the Lord's doing, and his only. It was an act of his power: Thy right hand, O Lord, not ours, has dashed in pieces the enemy
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

cites.quote: On this score, he repeats twice the mention of God’s “right hand;” as much as to say that such a miracle could not be ascribed either to fortune or to the efforts of man.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)

notes.short: Evening and morning: to “know” is to “see”
notes.about: Two matching lines: evening answers morning, and “know” answers “see.” Read together, they can be taken as one promise: evening and morning alike, Israel would see and know the glory of the LORD who brought them out, in the meat and bread He would give (verse 8).

lines.words: This evening you will know that it was the LORD who brought you out of the land of Egypt,
and in the morning you will see the LORD’s glory,

notes.evidence: Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) reads the two clauses as parallel: seeing is the same as knowing, and in the evening and in the morning alike Israel would perceive the glory of the LORD who brought them out, in His gift of meat and bread.
notes.limit: Others take the evening and the morning as two signs, the quail and then the manna, or the glory as the cloud of verse 10.

cites.quote: Bearing in mind the parallelism of the clauses, we obtain this meaning, that in the evening and in the morning the Israelites would perceive the glory of the Lord, who had brought them out of Egypt. "Seeing" is synonymous with "knowing." ... in their perception or experience of that glory in the miraculous gift of flesh and bread
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

notes.short: “For each person”: in Hebrew, “for a skull”
notes.about: Where the BSB says each person, the Hebrew counts skulls: an omer to a skull. One part of a man, his skull, stands for the whole man, as we say so much per head.

figure.name: Synecdoche
figure.means: an omer per head: the skull, one part of a man, is named for the whole man

original.note: In Hebrew the word is gulgoleth, a skull.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Synecdoche of the Part in Figures of Speech, where the skull, a part of the man, is put for the man himself: the Hebrew reads an omer a skull, that is, an omer per head.

cites.quote: “An omer a skull”: i.e., an omer per head
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

notes.short: The LORD “relented”: told in human words
notes.about: Moses pleads, and the LORD relents from the calamity He had threatened. Scripture tells it in the words used of a man who turns from what he meant to do, so that we can understand God. The same Bible says He “is not a man, that He should change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29).

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's sparing His people at Moses' plea, told as a man turns from what he meant to do

original.note: In Hebrew “relented” is nacham, the same word Moses used in verse 12 when he asked the LORD to “relent”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the verse under Anthropopatheia, where repentance is spoken of God. Keil (Keil and Delitzsch) calls it an anthropopathic picture of the pain caused to God's love. Clarke says it is said after the manner of men, Rawlinson (Ellicott) that the speech is anthropomorphic, and Calvin that with God repentance is only a change of dealing: He was appeased and did not do as He had said.
notes.limit: The writers agree the word is a figure, but differ on whether it tells of real pain in God's love or only of a change in how He dealt with His people.

cites.quote: Human affections and feelings are attributed to God: not that He has such feelings; but, in infinite condescension, He is thus spoken of in order to enable us to comprehend Him. ... Repentance is attributed to God.
cites.read: the UniqueBible.app module of the 1898 text, at github.com/darrelwright/UniqueBible_Books (commit 4017a67)

cites.quote: the deep spiritual idea of the repentance of God, as an anthropopathic description of the pain which is caused to the love of God by the destruction of His creatures
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: This is spoken merely after the manner of men who, having formed a purpose, permit themselves to be diverted from it by strong and forcible reasons, and so change their minds relative to their former intentions.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: He is, therefore, said to have “repented”; not that He had really changed His purpose, for He had known from the beginning that Moses would intercede and that He would spare, but because He first announced a (conditional) purpose, and then announced a different one. The mode of speech is, as so frequently, anthropomorphic.
cites.read: StudyLight's transcription, in the MyBible module at github.com/batanus/bible-resources (commit 14a8b1a)

cites.quote: But with God repentance is nothing but a change of dealing, wherein He seems to retrace His course, as if He had conceived some fresh design. ... it is tantamount to saying, that He was appeased; not because He retracts in Himself what He has once decreed, but because He does not execute the sentence He had pronounced.
cites.read: Let's Church's copy, at github.com/LetsChurch/lets.church (commit 71f6f0f)
